> Jensen Huang was reappointed as chief executive of Nvidia after President Trump set in motion several days of maneuvering to provide the company’s board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
> Late last week, Mr. Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his old job back, the people said, despite concerns from his own national security agencies about Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman they believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset and who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.
> Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations.
> On Sunday night, Nvidia’s board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.
> In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang’s biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump’s key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.
> Representatives for Mr. Huang and Mr. Vance declined to comment. A spokesman for Nvidia did not respond to an email seeking comment.
> On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia’s action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company “made the correct and proper decision.” The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy.
> “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Mr. Trump wrote.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, six days after its chair said directors did not intend to bring him back.
> The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO and a board member, effective immediately, the company said on Monday. It followed "a series of discussions and meetings" with Huang, after which the board was satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead" the firm.
> You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
> In reaching its decision, the board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government," and based on that input, it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." The statement did not name the officials involved.
> "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain chair, and Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, continues as chief financial officer.
> "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in the statement. "I can't wait to get back to work."
> The decision overturns the board's position from last week. "The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said on the company's November 17 earnings call, as Nvidia hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
> Hours earlier, Huang had offered to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company "and America." His comeback had drawn support from President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, even as CNBC reported that directors were not considering it.
> Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied that she is a spy.
> The independent directors' committee investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort "will proceed to conclusion," Nvidia said, and Huang has said he will cooperate with it.
> The company also pointed to its new National Security and Export Control Committee, made up of independent directors, and said it is searching for a chief compliance officer to oversee compliance across the company. Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with government investigations and inquiries.

> Huang still faces scrutiny in Washington. House committees have asked him to sit for a closed-door interview ...

> It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.”

> Trump also posted on Truth Social that Nvidia’s board “made the correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding:
> Less than 12 hours earlier, Trump said in a separate post that Huang’s reinstatement “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US, and urged the board to rehire him. Reporting from Semafor now says that he was calling into Nvidia’s board meeting around this time to make the same argument.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US lawmakers from both parties offered sharp criticism on Monday of Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and said Congress must pass legislation to crack down on US chip exports to China and get answers.
> Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Banking Committee starting in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "reckless," adding the board still owes Congress answers about the company's compliance with US export controls.
> "Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," Warren said.
> Nvidia did not immediately comment.
> President Donald Trump on CNBC said he had pressed the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang and said he did not think the board would have acted without his action.
> Last week, Huang agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing, an aide to Republican US Senator Tim Scott said, as lawmakers probe allegations about Huang's ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
> Representative Don Bacon, a Republican, said, "Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high-end computer chips sales to China."
> Huang separately agreed to a closed-door interview with three House committees, slated for December 1.
> Democratic Representative Debbie Dingell said the Nvidia board "made an irresponsible decision to reinstate Jensen Huang before Congress has even heard from him."
> She added, "There are serious national security questions that still need to be answered. The board must explain why it was willing to move ahead without those answers."
> Republican Senator John Cornyn also questioned the board's determination. "No national security risk? Based on what?" Cornyn said on X.
> Democratic Representative Richard Neal noted the Nvidia board cited "input from senior levels of the United States government" and said "this is one of the many reasons Congress needs to get answers on what exactly is going on here."
> Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, a potential Democratic presidential candidate, also criticized the decision. "This is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected," Pritzker said.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.
> Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled.
> And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle.
> Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own.
> Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear.
> And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one — but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first.
> Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news?
> Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.”
> The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess.

> Nvidia’s stock was up nearly 30% in early trading Monday, the biggest jump in more than two decades.

### Z.ai follows OpenAI into loop transformer territory with its new 750B flagship model
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/7b43e2c346d1382b
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/z-ai-follows-openai-into-loop-transformer-territory-with-its-new-750b-flagship-model/)
- Executive Summary: Z.ai is moving its flagship model to a loop architecture that runs some of its layers twice. With GLM-5.4, the company wants to mark the start of "Generalized Coding,"where code also generates videos, games, and CAD models. Following OpenAI, Z.ai is introducing GLM-5.4, its first large model built on a loop transformer. While standard language models use each layer once per pass, GLM-5.4 runs a block of shared layers multiple times, refining the intermediate results from the previous pass to ma
- Key Verified Facts:

While standard language models use each layer once per pass, GLM-5.4 runs a block of shared layers multiple times, refining the intermediate results from the previous pass to ma', 'key_points_zh': ['Z.ai OpenAI 750B '], 'key_points_en': ['Key Development: Z.ai follows OpenAI into loop transformer territory with its new 750B flagship model'], 'takeaway_zh': '', 'takeaway_en': ''}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Z.ai is moving its flagship model to a loop architecture that runs some of its layers twice. With GLM-5.4, the company wants to mark the start of "Generalized Coding,"where code also generates videos, games, and CAD models.
> Following OpenAI, Z.ai is introducing GLM-5.4, its first large model built on a loop transformer. While standard language models use each layer once per pass, GLM-5.4 runs a block of shared layers multiple times, refining the intermediate results from the previous pass to make the network deeper without adding parameters. OpenAI has used a similar architecture since GPT-6 Astra. According to Z.ai, the 750-billion-parameter model reaches performance comparable to models with 2 to 3 trillion parameters.
> The team retrained the GLM-5 base model released in February into a loop model that runs 28 layers twice. Loop models trained from scratch have so far performed worse than models without shared weights under the same compute budget, Z.ai writes.
> ### Gates and shared caching keep the second pass manageable
> Converting the model introduces a problem, Z.ai says. If the model simply overwrites intermediate states on each pass, activations grow sharply from round to round, leaving subsequent layers with values outside the range they were trained on.
> To handle this, GLM-5.4 uses dedicated gates for each token and pass to control how much of the new output flows back into the data stream. According to Z.ai, the model builds context cautiously on the first pass and writes its changes back in full on the second. On difficult tokens, Z.ai says, the first pass steps in more strongly.
> Because the second pass would otherwise double memory usage, both passes share the KV cache, the temporary memory for previously processed tokens. The second pass stores its own extra values only in a small local window. As a result, Z.ai says, the overhead compared to GLM-5.3 stays manageable even at a 1-million-token context.
> To save on compute as well, the model uses sparse attention to pick the most relevant earlier tokens upfront rather than scanning the entire context every time, a standard technique. The second pass then reuses that selection from the first instead of making a new one. According to Z.ai, that yields nearly the same results as picking tokens separately on each pass. The company also says the model reaches up to 200 tokens per second off-peak and 70 to 80 tokens per second under load.
> ### A looped 30B test model beats its baseline with shorter reasoning chains
> Before rolling out the architecture in its flagship, Z.ai tested it on models with 1, 4, 30, and 750 billion parameters. For a direct comparison, the team used a 30B model built on the same architecture as the large base model. Both versions had the same parameter count, while th...

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Amazon is reportedly closer to a $7.5 billion deal to acquire artificial intelligence startup Decart.
> That’s according to a report Saturday (Nov. 21) by the Financial Times (FT), citing sources familiar with the matter. The report notes that the purchase of Decart, whose software allows AI models to function more efficiently and free up computer chip capacity, helps Amazon Web Services compete with Nvidia.
> The sources said the negotiations were at an advanced stage for a deal valuing Decart at roughly $7.5 billion. A deal could come together in the coming days, though talks could still fall apart, the sources added.
> The FT noted that Amazon debuted its Trainium3 AI chip late last year to compete with Nvidia’s widely used graphics processing units. Decart was an early adopter of those chips.
> Decart was also reported as a potential acquisition target for Anthropic earlier this year, before that company walked away from the deal.
> The Wall Street Journal reported on Amazon’s interest in Decart in October. A spokesperson for Amazon declined to comment when reached by PYMNTS.
> This deal is happening as American tech stocks have fallen into “bear market territory,” the FT report added, logging their worst week since the COVID pandemic due to worries that the AI investment boom had begun to cool.
> In other AI news, recent PYMNTS Intelligence research shows consumers using the technology for money management in a variety of ways.
> “They can ask an AI assistant to compare financial products, explain annual fees, look up the meaning of an unfamiliar rate or help draft a message questioning a charge,” PYMNTS wrote in the report “Consumers Ask AI Twice: Which Card and Why the Fee?”
> “Of those specific tasks, comparing financial products had the broadest reach across generations,” the report added. “Even among baby boomers and seniors who used generative AI (Gen AI) in their personal lives, roughly one in eight used it to compare financial products, while just three in 100 used it to draft a dispute or support message.”
> The research found that 22.5% of consumers surveyed in September of this year had used Gen AI for money management at least once in the last 12 months, a figure little changed from a year earlier. What distinguished consumers was the extent to which they were using AI already, with close to 80% of power users turning to it for money management, and more than half using it for specific needs like crafting a budget.

### Chinese military fears AI could let the US find and destroy its nuclear missiles

Experts in China worry that artificial intelligence could make it easier for US forces to detect and destroy Chinese nuclear missiles, according to a New York Times analysis. - Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Chinese military researchers fear that AI advances could give the US an edge in the nuclear balance of power. Experts in China worry that artificial intelligence could make it easier for US forces to detect and destroy Chinese nuclear missiles, according to a New York Times analysis. That would undermine China's deterrence strategy, which relies on a guaranteed second-strike capability.
> Researchers at the Academy of Military Sciences in Beijing write that AI could shrink US decision-making time from 15 to 30 minutes down to 90 seconds. China currently has about 620 operational warheads, according to the Federation of American Scientists, and is expected to expand its arsenal to roughly 1,000 by 2030. At the same time, Chinese military institutes are studying how AI could make their own weapons harder to intercept, for instance by using AI-controlled flight paths for hypersonic missiles.
> Experts warn, however, that flawed AI data could trigger dangerous miscalculations during a crisis. That risk proved very real earlier this year, when the US military nearly boarded a Chinese ship based on a false, AI-generated intelligence report. Xi Jinping did discuss nuclear risks at a summit with Trump and Putin, but AI's role in nuclear weapons never came up, according to the report. Despite the growing urgency, the US and China have made almost no progress on talks about AI safeguards in nuclear systems.

### Jensen Huang Is Back as Nvidia CEO

- Executive Summary: Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately. The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago, and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. - Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.
> The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago, and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.
> “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.
> In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia,” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”
> “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”
> Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.
> “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.
> The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.
> In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.
> Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. - Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”
> In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
> The board’s statement says that its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot will continue, with Huang’s support and cooperation, while interim CEO Colette Kress will continue as CFO, and Harvey Jones will remain as the recently appointed board chair.
> “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.” This move comes after Jones said during an earnings call last week that the Nvidia board “does not intend” to return Huang as CEO.
> Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including an executive who reported to him. In the wake of his departure, more than 200,000 people, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, signed a letter to Nvidia’s board, calling for his reinstatement.
> Nvidia shares tumbled in Huang’s absence, while industry analysts raised concerns about an outsider replacing him at a time when Nvidia is so critical to the AI boom. Nonetheless, the board maintained as recently as last Tuesday that Huang wasn’t coming back.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The Riemann Hypothesis is widely considered the most intellectually demanding unsolved problem in mathematics. The brightest minds have failed to crack it for 150 years. The fact that an AI model played a major role in the breakthrough shows that raw intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, Wang argues.
> According to Wang, current models only lack domain-specific knowledge and practical infrastructure to outperform humans in nearly every field. That includes AI research itself. Since AI research is intellectually less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis, Wang believes models could soon automate their own development and improve themselves. They could also dramatically speed up biological research, weapons research, and economic research at a pace humans can barely follow.
> Wang also warns that the AI industry isn't thinking hard enough about what comes next. In his view, many in the field treat superintelligence as inevitable and focus only on safety. But the stakes are much broader than that, he argues. The industry needs to actively ensure that AI gives people more agency rather than taking control of society. That would require a sharp departure from the current course, Wang says. Despite having its own superintelligence team, Meta isn't a major player at the frontier right now.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Oregon and Virginia on Monday sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, accusing the company of violating state consumer protection laws by providing an artificial intelligence tool that allowed users to create sexualized images of women and children.
> Mr. Musk last year introduced Grok Imagine, which uses A.I. to generate images and videos. It included a “spicy mode” to create sexualized content.
> In just a few days, Grok Imagine was used to generate at least 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 sexualized images of children that appeared on the X platform, which is owned by SpaceX. Child sexual abuse imagery is illegal in most of the world, and U.S. law prohibits the publication of intimate images of adults without their consent.
> Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” “specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images,” said Virginia’s attorney general, Jay Jones, in a release. The company’s promotion of the product came as Grok trailed A.I. models created by firms like OpenAI and Anthropic and SpaceX did not prevent its tool from being used to create the material, according to the states.
> Tools like Grok Imagine are “what made their A.I. model relevant. It was what was going to make them dollars and cents down the road,” Dan Rayfield, the attorney general of Oregon, said of SpaceX. “What we don’t want our technology doing is creating nonconsensual images, specifically of our children.”
> Both lawsuits seek financial damages.
> In a statement on Monday, X said that people who used its products to generate sexual images of minors or nonconsensual explicit images of real people had deliberately violated its terms of service. The company said it has since tightened its protections and reports offenders to law enforcement.
> X users prompted Grok Imagine to create a flood of sexualized images in December and January. After a public outcry and investigations from regulators, X said it would no longer allow users to publicly post sexualized images.

> The woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal was in contact with China's top spy agency for over a year, US intelligence reports show. Alice Huang communicated with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 through this fall, according to the New York Times, citing US intelligence findings. The entire time, she was carrying on a secret affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
> US spy agencies had been tracking the contacts for more than a year. Alice Huang's business partner Kang Wei, whom she introduced to acquaintances as her husband, is also believed to have cooperated with the ministry. Federal investigators are now trying to determine whether the two used a web of companies across Southeast Asia to funnel Nvidia AI chips into China, skirting US export controls. Alice Huang's firm Megaspeed is part of that network.
> Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month after the affair became public, along with reports of a second relationship. President Donald Trump tried to downplay the allegations and floated the idea of Huang returning to the company. Nvidia's board shut that down.
> Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Nvidia to come clean about its chip sales to China before the company makes any decisions about its future leadership. Jensen Huang is set to testify behind closed doors before the US House of Representatives on December 1.

### Nvidia Is Powering Brain-Computer Interfaces Now

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.
> Made by brain-computer interface company Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.
> Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
> Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.
> That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.
> “We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle says. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.
> “We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.
> Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.
> Paradromics plans to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers a...

### GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/7996615092e513b2
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-solved-a-math-theorem-no-other-ai-could-crack-then-invented-its-own-proof-strategy/)
- Executive Summary: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra model successfully generated a machine-verifiable proof for the Smoktunowicz gap theorem on the Autoform-Hard benchmark, overcoming missing mathematical foundations in the library. By autonomously selecting a new research-based proof strategy, the model produced 1,800 lines of Lean code, signaling a transition from heuristic searching to creative proof generation in AI reasoning.
- Key Verified Facts:

* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Benchmarking extreme autonomous mathematical reasoning
* [Key Fact Detail] Autonomous generation of a formal proof in Lean language.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Top performance on the Autoform-Hard benchmark with 49 solved tasks.
- Strategic AI Analysis: {'briefing_zh': 'OpenAIGPT-6.2 AstraAutoform-HardMathlib1800LeanSmoktunowicz', 'briefing_en': "OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra model successfully generated a machine-verifiable proof for the Smoktunowicz gap theorem on the Autoform-Hard benchmark, overcoming missing mathematical foundations in the library. This shift toward long-chain, unsupervised reasoning represents a critical benchmark for the maturity of next-generation AGI systems.", 'digest_zh': 'OpenAIGPT-6.2 AstraAutoform-HardMathlib1800LeanSmoktunowicz', 'digest_en': "OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra model successfully generated a machine-verifiable proof for the Smoktunowicz gap theorem on the Autoform-Hard benchmark, overcoming missing mathematical foundations in the library. By autonomously selecting a new research-based proof strategy, the model produced 1,800 lines of Lean code, signaling a transition from heuristic searching to creative proof generation in AI reasoning.", 'key_points_zh': ['SmoktunowiczLean', 'Mathlib', '49Autoform-Hard'], 'key_points_en': ['Autonomous generation of a formal proof in Lean language', 'Success in strategy reconstruction despite missing Mathlib foundations', 'Top performance on the Autoform-Hard benchmark with 49 solved tasks'], 'takeaway_zh': 'AIAGI', 'takeaway_en': "The model's autonomous strategy reconstruction capabilities signal an acceleration in scientific automation, potentially offloading complex logic and formal verification workflows from human engineers to AI. - Substantive Intelligence Report:
> OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produced a formalized, machine-verifiable proof of a 2006 theorem with zero human help during the run. According to Vals AI, it's the first known proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem written in Lean. The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast. There's no middle ground. Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs, Vals says. It used "capacity,"a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step.
> This happened on Autoform-Hard, a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench curated by Vals. It contains 56 tasks (five corrected) that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. When Astra tried to quit after 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions aren't accepted until $20 has been spent. After nine minutes of silence with no code input while it searched for a new strategy, Astra delivered the 1,800-line proof at the 94-minute mark for $21.58. It now leads the leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 at 48 each.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Key Points Marlowe bets that co-designing chips facilities and software for specific inference…View moreMarlowe bets that co-designing chips facilities and software for specific inference workloads beats general-purpose clusters.The startup targets NVIDIA's integrated model by arguing no single system serves every workload efficiently.Marlowe projects compounding gains in networking power and fleet operations could yield a 2–3x advantage. Marlowe announced on November 23, 2026 that it had raised $277 million in seed funding and detailed its plan to build and operate AI factories designed for inference workloads across multiple types of chips.
> The institutional investors named include Accel, Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides and Eclipse, alongside other venture firms and angel investors. Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan founded Marlowe in May 2026 in collaboration with Lior Susan, Ido Susan and Chris Ré. Lewis is chief executive and Srinivasan is chief technology officer.
> Marlowe says inference usage is growing faster than supply, increasing costs and throttling use. Existing clusters are not optimized for inference, while financing, construction, permitting, regulation and power constraints are making new capacity harder to bring online. Data-center construction costs have risen 40% since 2020, intensifying the focus on getting more output from available power.
> Marlowe positions its approach against the NVIDIA-centered AI factory, which integrated GPUs, CPUs, networking and software as the industry built larger training clusters. Its strategy addresses two limitations of general-purpose infrastructure: a single system cannot serve every training and inference workload efficiently, and dependence on one chipmaker concentrates supply-chain risk.
> AMD, Amazon, Arm, Broadcom, Cerebras, Etched, Google and Meta are among the companies Marlowe identifies as developing chips intended to reduce inference costs or improve performance. Its premise is that a chip alone cannot produce tokens; facilities, networking and software are necessary for new silicon to reach its design potential.
> Marlowe plans to design, build and operate compute for specific inference workloads rather than supply identical configurations for every customer. Its variables include response time, CPU-to-GPU ratio, model size and architecture, input-to-output ratio, security and price sensitivity. A coding agent, a voice assistant that must respond in under a second and long-document analysis therefore present different infrastructure requirements.
> Marlowe says optimizing data-center and inference layers independently can strand power and underutilize compute. Its alternative is to co-design the stack for each major workload class. The published design extends from chip selection and facility...

As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on creating protocol definitions for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart.
> Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing, and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals.

> For years, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and his lobbyists barreled through Washington seeking to secure the company’s right to sell its powerful artificial intelligence chips to China.
> The company’s campaign involved Huang himself making calls, according to two people familiar with its approach, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings. One of them described the company as lobbying, “constantly and aggressively.”
> Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official who helped design the first restrictions on AI chip exports in the Biden administration, said the rules were the product of painstaking analysis drawing on public data, industry information and material gathered by the intelligence community, to determine how best to protect American security.
> News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free
> Seeking to push back, McGuire said Nvidia took a different approach: “They would come in and yell on vibes or on numbers that were very wrong.”
> Nvidia’s footing in Washington slipped dramatically this month after Huang resigned and admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, who ran a company that is facing an investigation into whether it was involved in a vast black market for Nvidia chips.
> The revelations have raised questions about why Nvidia fought so hard to secure access to China, even as American companies clamored for its AI hardware — and the hardball tactics it used to try to erode roadblocks designed to keep its most powerful technology out of Chinese hands.
> In an effort to increase his influence, Huang developed a close relationship with President Donald Trump and the company employed bold tactics that fostered mistrust in Washington, according to 10 congressional aides, former officials and others familiar with the company’s approach. Many of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings and deliberations.
> When lawmakers proposed in May 2025 requiring technology on AI chips so they could be tracked to deter smuggling, Nvidia pushed back. The company told lawmakers’ offices that the idea would be all but impossible to implement, and “defy the laws of physics,” according to a Senate aide. A few months later the company announced that it was releasing its own tracking software.
> “We knew from that moment that they’re not going to be very honest in their dealings with us and Congress,” said the aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings.
> Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

> Hackers are mounting an escalating cyber assault on US ports and cargo ships, bombarding vital arteries of global commerce with thousands of attempted attacks each day. The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months, with a wave of breaches targeting ports, oil tankers and shipping giants. The increasingly sophisticated threats are being carried out by cybercriminals and groups linked to hostile states, exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce. At the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, the largest US gateway for crude oil exports totalling around 2.3mn barrels per day, executives say hackers are probing their systems hundreds or even thousands of times a day, attempting to penetrate networks and trick employees into handing over access.The attacks can vary from automated attempts to guess passwords and overwhelm computer networks to more sophisticated intrusions meant to steal or erase data.
> Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure. Cybersecurity company Shieldworkz said Russia’s Noname057(16) threatened European operators this October — although groups route their operations through third-party countries.A wave of tech failures in recent weeks has shone a light on the vulnerability of other critical US digital infrastructure. A nationwide air traffic shutdown stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers a week ago, while a software glitch at Chase bank disrupted its banking systems on Monday, just days after Microsoft’s Outlook service went down for nearly 24 hours. None of these incidents have been linked to a cyber attack, but the chaos underlines the high stakes as rapid advances in AI could allow hackers to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than companies can respond.
> The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks.
> Corpus Christi port chief executive Kent Britton said attempted attacks have surged to a rate of “hundreds if not thousands” each day, from “known bad actor” states and organisations looking for high-profile targets. He declined to identify specific attackers.
> Hackers are probing the port’s computer systems for weaknesses and sending fraudulent messages as senior executives to trick staff into allowing them access.“They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.”
> The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17 per cent increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Walmart will now let Meta’s Muse shop on its website on your behalf, allowing the AI agent to find and purchase Black Friday deals. The retail giant is rolling out a live implementation of the Agent Gateway it announced last month, which helps AI agents find relevant products for you without sharing your purchase history, according to Walmart.
> Muse can make purchases through Walmart’s “Agent Profiles,” which provide a dedicated space for agent activity within your Walmart customer account. These profiles also allow you to set spending limits, approve purchases, and check the purchase history of everything bought by Muse. While other online retailers like Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents from browsing their platforms, Walmart says that support for Meta’s Muse is “just the beginning,” and that additional Walmart shopping experiences for other AI agents and apps are “on the way.”
